hook.line: Back in Bogotá, Tomás and Vale can't keep up alone, so they tape their first job ad to the café window. Signs like that don't say who wants anything. Spanish has a tiny word for that: *se*.

examples.es: En este café se come muy bien.
examples.en: You eat really well in this café.

examples.es: En Bogotá se toma mucho tinto.
examples.en: In Bogotá people drink a lot of black coffee.

rule:
Sometimes nobody in particular is doing the action. English fills the gap with you, people, one, or a passive: English is spoken here, you eat well here.

Spanish just puts *se* in front of the he/she form of the verb:
*se habla*: is spoken, people speak
*se necesita*: is needed
*se come*: you eat, people eat
*se puede*: you can, it's OK to

The verb stays in the he/she form whoever you mean, because you don't mean anyone. Without *se*, it's about one person: *Necesita mesero* is he or she needs a waiter.

*No* goes before *se*: *No se habla inglés*. After *se puede*, the next verb is the dictionary form: *¿Se puede pagar con tarjeta?*

With more than one thing, the verb goes plural: *se vende carro*, but *se venden carros*.
smallPrint: Teachers call this the impersonal *se* (and, when the verb agrees with a thing, the passive *se*). It's how signs, ads and rules talk.

readAndPick.es: En Bogotá se toma mucho tinto.
options: In Bogotá he drinks a lot of black coffee.
In Bogotá people drink a lot of black coffee.

readAndPick.es: En este café se come muy bien.
options: You eat really well in this café.
She eats really well in this café.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *se necesita* or *necesita* and type the whole sentence. A sign in the café window: ___ mesero.
yourTurn.why: A sign isn't about one person, so it takes *se*.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *se habla* or *habla* and type the whole sentence. A sign by the door: Aquí ___ inglés.
yourTurn.why: Nobody in particular is speaking, so *se* goes in front.

yourTurn.prompt: Write a sign for a shop: Spanish spoken here.
Write an ad for your car: Car for sale.
yourTurn.why: For sale is *se vende*, the he/she form with *se*.

yourTurn.prompt: Ask the waiter whether people can pay by card here.
yourTurn.why: *Se puede* asks if it's OK in general, and the next verb stays in its dictionary form.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative: *Aquí se habla inglés.*
yourTurn.why: *No* goes in front of *se*, never between *se* and the verb.

yourTurn.prompt: Turn it into a fact about everyone, not just Tomás: *Tomás come muy bien en este café.*
yourTurn.answer: En este café se come muy bien.
accept: Se come muy bien en este café.
yourTurn.why: Drop the person and put *se* in front of the verb.

pitfalls.why: Almost. *Ellos* means some particular people; for people in general, Spanish uses *se*.
Without *se*, it says she or he needs a waiter, not that the café does.
English says is sold or for sale, but Spanish doesn't build it that way: it just puts *se* in front, *se vende*.
After *se puede*, the next verb stays in its dictionary form.

personal: Write two signs for a place you know well (your home, your office or your street): one thing people do there and one thing you can't do. *En mi casa se come…* and *En mi oficina no se puede…*
